definition: In multi-armed bandit problems, KL-UCB (for Kullback–Leibler Upper Confidence Bound) is a UCB-type algorithm that is asymptotically optimal, in the sense that its regret matches the problem-dependent Lai-Robbins lower bound..
details: In multi-armed bandit problems, KL-UCB (for Kullback–Leibler Upper Confidence Bound) is a UCB-type algorithm that is asymptotically optimal, in the sense that its regret matches the problem-dependent Lai-Robbins lower bound.

explainer.lead: KL-UCB is a bandit algorithm whose regret provably approaches the best any algorithm can achieve. That asymptotic optimality makes it a benchmark for how efficiently an algorithm can learn which option is best.

tiers.eli5: When picking between slot machines, you keep a score for each and lean toward ones that might be better than they look; KL-UCB is the version of that strategy that wastes the fewest tries in the long run.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it when regret matters and reward distributions are Bernoulli, since its confidence bounds are built on KL divergence between estimated and candidate means. A pitfall is that its index is harder to compute than plain UCB and needs an inner optimization.
tiers.paperLevel: For each arm, the index is the largest mean q such that the number of observations times the KL divergence between the empirical mean and q stays below a log-based threshold; its regret matches the Lai-Robbins lower bound asymptotically. The guarantee is asymptotic and problem-dependent, not a finite-sample bound.

explainer.example: For an arm pulled 100 times with empirical mean 0.4, the index is the highest q whose KL divergence from 0.4, scaled by 100, still fits under the confidence threshold.
